mainEntity.name: How much does a Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi engine replacement cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi engine replacement typically costs £1,800-£4,000 supply-only for a rebuilt unit, depending on engine code (F9Q 804 / F9Q 812 / F9Q 870). Used engines start from £400-£1,400. Fitting adds approximately £650-£1,040 in labour (10-16 hours at independent specialist rates). Main dealer fitted prices are typically 30-50% higher.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of turbo failure in a Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common signs include loss of power, black smoke from the exhaust, a whistling or screeching noise from the turbo, and increased oil consumption. A faulty EGR valve is often the root cause - it either sticks open or closed, causing premature turbo failure. If you notice any of these symptoms, have the turbo and EGR inspected immediately.

mainEntity.name: Why does my Scenic 1.9 dCi show a "check injection" warning?

acceptedAnswer.text: The "check injection" warning is commonly caused by injector failure. Injector leak-off (excessive fuel return) is a common symptom. If ignored, injector failure can lead to high-pressure fuel pump failure, which can contaminate the entire fuel system and result in a £7,000 repair bill.

mainEntity.name: What is the timing belt interval for a Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi?

acceptedAnswer.text: The 1.9 dCi F9Q engine uses a timing belt (not a chain). The official replacement interval is typically 72,000 miles or 5 years - whichever comes first. A failed water pump bearing can cause the belt to track incorrectly, leading to catastrophic engine failure.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in a Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a Scenic II (2003-2009) worth £800-£3,000, a rebuilt engine at £1,800-£4,000 plus fitting may represent 80-120% of the vehicle's value. If the car is otherwise in good condition with a strong gearbox and low rust, a used engine or targeted repair may be more cost-effective. For Scenic III (2009-2016) worth £2,000-£6,000, a rebuilt engine may represent 50-80% of the vehicle's value. For Grand Scenic seven-seat models (£2,500-£8,000+), replacement is usually viable due to family demand.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between the 8-valve and 16-valve 1.9 dCi engines?

acceptedAnswer.text: The earlier Scenic I and early Scenic II 1.9 dCi used an 8-valve SOHC design (F9Q 740, F9Q 804, F9Q 812). Later Scenic II and Scenic III models used a 16-valve DOHC design (F9Q 870, F9Q 872). The 16-valve engine produces more power (131hp vs 102-120hp) and is generally more refined, but has more complex emissions systems (DPF, AdBlue on later models) and can be more expensive to repair. Both use a timing belt, not a chain.

historyTimeline.h2: Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi arrived in 1999 with the first-generation Scenic I, establishing itself as the torque-rich diesel alternative to the smaller 1.5 dCi across Scenic I, II and III generations. The 1.9 dCi engine family was available in two valvetrain configurations - 8-valve (SOHC) and 16-valve (DOHC) - with power outputs ranging from 102hp to 131hp. The engine was particularly popular in Grand Scenic seven-seat models, where the extra torque was valued for carrying heavier loads. Production of the Scenic 1.9 dCi ended with the Scenic IV introduction in 2016, replaced by the 1.6 dCi (R9M) and 2.0 dCi (M9R).

commonProblems.h2: Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi (F9Q family) is a torquey, common-rail diesel that powered Scenic I, II and III across a 17-year production run. While the engine is capable of high mileage, it has well-documented failure points - turbocharger failure (often linked to EGR issues), injector failure, high-pressure fuel pump failure and DPF/EGR problems. The earlier 8-valve variants are generally simpler and more robust than the later higher-output versions, but all require diligent maintenance. Rebuilt Scenic 1.9 dCi engines through EnginesMarket include upgraded components addressing the original failure points, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: Turbocharger Failure - Why the Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi Suffers Premature Turbo Death
problems.affectedModels: Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi (F9Q 740 / F9Q 804 / F9Q 812 / F9Q 870, 1999-2016)
problems.typicalFailureMileage: 60,000-100,000 miles (turbo should last 150,000 miles but rarely does due to neglect)
problems.rootCause: A faulty EGR valve - either stuck open or closed - causes premature turbo failure. Turbo pipe splits are also reported, particularly on Scenic I models. Turbocharger failure is so common that it was one of the most frequent warranty claims on early Scenic 1.9 dCi models. Oil starvation from blocked oil feed lines can also destroy the turbo.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove, replace turbo, new oil feed lines, clean EGR
repairOptions.longevity: If turbo has failed but engine is otherwise healthy

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace EGR valve, inspect turbo, clear codes
repairOptions.longevity: If caught early before turbo damage occurs
When turbo failure has caused catastrophic damage

problems.recommendation: For any Scenic 1.9 dCi owner, preventative maintenance is critical. Check the EGR valve regularly - a failing EGR will kill the turbo. Use premium diesel and ensure DPF regens are completed - short urban journeys are the enemy. If you see "check injection" warning or rough running, get injectors tested immediately. For Scenic II models worth under £1,500, a used engine may be more economically sensible than a rebuilt unit.

problems.h4: Injector & High-Pressure Fuel Pump Failure - Fuel System Weakness
problems.rootCause: Injector failure causes rough running, "check injection" warnings and running on three cylinders. Injector leak-off (excessive return flow) is a common symptom. High-pressure fuel pump failure can cause metal particles to contaminate the entire fuel system - Renault's official fix is to replace the whole system including injectors and sensors, which can produce a bill of £7,000.

For Scenic II models worth under £1,500, a used engine may be more economically sensible than a rebuilt unit.

problems.h4: DPF & EGR System Problems - Emissions Equipment Failures
problems.affectedModels: Renault Scenic 1.9 dCi (Euro 4 / Euro 5 variants, F9Q 804 / F9Q 812 / F9Q 870, 2003-2016)
problems.rootCause: The Scenic 1.9 dCi's DPF system, particularly on early Grand Scenic models, is known to be problematic. DPF regeneration requires sustained high RPM driving - typically 10 minutes above 3,000rpm for the regen to take place. Pressure sensor pipes can develop holes, causing the DPF to block as quickly as it's cleaned. EGR valve clogging is also common, creating more soot and accelerating DPF blockage.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Diagnostic forced regen or chemical clean

repairOptions.longevity: If DPF is blocked beyond cleaning

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove, clean or replace EGR valve
